Here's the trick with mouse traps. Typically, the metal sensor will have a loop shape to it. You want to tuck the bait in as far as you can leave and very minimal access to the food. This will still produce the smell but won't offer a free meal. Second, mice are creatures of habit and will run along the same courses. You can often detect these courses by inspecting your baseboards for any oily residue or streaks with no dust. Put the trap facing along the wall. When they're used to their route, they run it pretty quickly. The trap may catch them before they realize it.

Living in the desert I have a constant problem with mice and packrats. They will build nests in my car's engine (using pieces of cactus...), chew through soil-cement, and I've woken up to discover my shoes filled with bird seed. And if you have too many rodents around they start attracting the snakes. But respiratory problems keep me from having pets so no cats. I've had the best luck with the Victor electronic rat traps. Though designed for rats, they work for everything from small mice to rats so large they won't completely fit inside them. And the battery usage is remarkably low. However, some rodents seem completely immune. Occasionally there will be one mouse that seems to be dielectric and won't set them off. Maybe the smaller size ones work better for them. They're a bit expensive, but I've found them on sale as they are slow movers in the stores. The company direct prices are, strangely, at least double their usual store and Amazon prices. Some new very expensive models now have systems to send you email and IMs when the trap goes off.
